content: The recommendations primarily emphasize the use of HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method for cervical cancer. Additionally, one recommendation addresses the types of triage tests that can be employed following a positive primary screening result. In December 2021, the first part of Phase 2 of the guideline update was published, introducing a recommendation for the use of HPV mRNA testing as a primary screening test. A comprehensive summary of these recommendations is available in the 2021 guidance document, which also includes relevant remarks and details in Annex 5. This document is intended for policymakers, program managers, program officers, and other health sector professionals responsible for selecting strategies for cervical cancer prevention at national, regional, and district levels. Health workers, including doctors, nurses, and community health workers involved in reproductive health programs, antenatal and postnatal services, family planning, HIV/AIDS control programs, and clinics caring for women at primary and district healthcare levels, may also consult this document. It provides insights into the development of evidence-based recommendations and highlights the importance of implementing such strategies to prevent cervical cancer. Furthermore, the document can serve as a foundation for creating adapted publications for women and their families to support informed decision-making regarding cervical cancer screening and treatment. The guideline acknowledges the right of all individuals to equality and non-discrimination in sexual and reproductive healthcare. While most evidence on cervical cancer is based on studies involving cisgender women, the guideline recognizes that transgender men, non-binary, gender-fluid, and intersex individuals with female reproductive systems also require cervical cancer prevention services. For simplicity and readability, the term women is used to refer to all gender-diverse individuals at risk for cervical cancer. The updated guideline was developed following the methods outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, second edition. Detailed methods are described in the publication of the first phase of the guideline update. This phase focuses on dual-stain cytology as a triage test. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), External Review Group (ERG), systematic review teams, modeling teams, and other contributors are listed in Annex 1, along with their expertise and affiliations. The WHO Secretariat, comprising staff from various WHO departments and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), coordinated the guideline's development. The GDG included 53 members (35 women, 18 men) from all six WHO regions, representing civil society organizations, women's groups, and women living with HIV. Two members served as co-chairs, moderating GDG meetings. Observers attended GDG meetings but did not participate in discussions or vote on recommendations. The ERG provided peer review for the guideline document, and its 18 members, with expertise in research, policy development, program implementation, and clinical care, reviewed the full draft and provided feedback. Evidence relevant to dual-stain cytology was prepared by multiple teams. Two teams conducted evidence reviews on the test accuracy of dual-stain cytology as a triage test for detecting CIN2+ and CIN3+ and on longitudinal evidence for its use. The GDG formulated recommendations using the GRADE approach, and conflicts of interest were managed through written declarations reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. Confidentiality agreements were signed by GDG members, and discussions and draft recommendations remained confidential until publication. Priority questions for dual-stain cytology were based on a scoping review and prioritization of research questions and algorithms for screening and treatment. The GDG identified seven priority algorithms for the first phase of the guideline update and four algorithms for HPV mRNA testing in the second phase. Two additional algorithms related to dual-stain cytology as a triage test following a positive HPV DNA or mRNA nucleic acid test result were addressed in this continuation of the second phase. Critical outcomes for screening and treatment recommendations include cervical cancer, mortality, high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN2+), HPV infection, preterm birth, pre-cancer treatments, adverse events (e.g., major infections, bleeding, pain, cervical stenosis, infertility, spontaneous abortion, perinatal deaths, premature rupture of membranes, unnecessary interventions, increased viral shedding in women living with HIV), costs, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Adverse events were defined as direct consequences of pre-cancer treatment, with preterm birth considered a critical outcome. Evidence was synthesized using methods from the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Both published and unpublished data were included in the literature review. Longitudinal studies, including unpublished ones identified through scientific meetings, were analyzed using prevalence-incidence mixture models. Dual-stain cytology was evaluated alone or in combination with partial HPV genotyping. A systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of dual-stain cytology compared to conventional cytology was conducted. Random-effects meta-analyses assessed the clinical sensitivity and specificity of dual-stain cytology and its relative performance compared to conventional cytology. Mathematical modeling using the Policy1-Cervix platform predicted outcomes in women across 78 lowand lower-middle-income countries. The model evaluated cervical cancer incidence, mortality, pre-cancer treatments, preterm deliveries, and cost-effectiveness. Sensitivity analyses varied the performance and cost of dual-stain cytology and considered rescreening intervals. Validation exercises demonstrated the model's accuracy in predicting dual-stain cytology performance as a triage test in HPV-positive women. A systematic review of values and preferences of end-users, health workers, and stakeholders informed the guideline development. Evidence was assessed using the GRADE-CERQual approach, and findings were summarized in the evidence-to-decision framework. Primary data from a voluntary survey of women aged 15 and older were also analyzed. Detailed methods and results are available in supplementary materials accompanying the guideline publication.
